title: Crown Appeal by Stated Case by Procurator Fiscal, Glasgow against Afaq Ahmad
text:
SHERIFF APPEAL COURT
[2026] SAC (Crim) 9
SAC/2026/178/AP

Sheriff Principal N Ross
Sheriff Principal A Miller
Appeal Sheriff W Sheehan

STATEMENT OF REASONS
delivered by SHERIFF PRINCIPAL ANDREW MILLER
in
Crown Appeal by Stated Case
by
PROCURATOR FISCAL, GLASGOW
Appellant
against
AFAQ AHMAD
Respondent
Appellant:  Fyfe, (sol adv), AD;  the Crown Agent
Respondent:  Culross, advocate;  John Pryde & Company, Edinburgh (for Richard Freeman &
Company, Glasgow
7 July 2026
[1]
On 7 July we heard the procurator fiscal’s appeal by stated case against the sheriff’s
decision to sustain a submission of no case to answer made on behalf of the respondent
during his summary trial for a contravention of section 5A(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1988.

2

The sole question for this court was whether the sheriff had erred in sustaining the
submission of no case to answer.
[2]
A number of matters were agreed by joint minute, including the fact that the
respondent was the driver of the vehicle concerned at the relevant time and the relevant
statutory procedures.  The only witness led by the Crown was a forensic toxicologist, who
spoke to the terms of a certificate produced for the purposes of section 16 of the Road Traffic
Offenders Act 1988 (“the Act”) and signed by him, setting out the results of the analysis of a
sample of the respondent’s blood.  The toxicologist’s evidence was led without objection and
was therefore evidence in causa (Skeen v Murphy 1978 SLT (Notes) 2).
[3]
The stated case indicated that the submission of no case to answer was presented on
the basis that, even though the toxicologist had given evidence about the matters set forth
in the certificate, that evidence could not amount to sufficient evidence of the results of the
analysis because the Crown had failed to prove service of the certificate on the respondent
in terms of section 16 of the Act.  Although the respondent’s solicitor had challenged the
certificate (for the purposes of section 16(4) of the Act) prior to the trial, he submitted that
the challenge had resulted from disclosure of the certificate to the solicitors, not from service
upon the respondent, and that it was only open to the Crown to rely on section 16(5)(a) of
the Act where the certificate had been served on the respondent.
[4]
In these circumstances, the procurator fiscal depute initially conceded that, as the
Crown had not produced an execution of service of the certificate on the respondent, there
was no case to answer and then, after an adjournment, revised her position and submitted
that the sheriff should repel the submission of no case to answer on the basis that “any
challenge to the service of a document should be made in advance of the trial.”

3

[5]
The sheriff sustained the submission on two grounds:  firstly, that the procurator
fiscal depute’s initial concession that there was no case to answer was binding on the
Crown;  and secondly that, before the Crown could rely on section 16(5)(a) of the Act, the
certificate setting out the results of the analysis required to be served on the respondent
in terms of section 16(5)(b), which the procurator fiscal depute could not confirm had
happened.  In the absence of proof of service, “any analysis relied upon by the crown
requires to be corroborated when that is the only evidence on the matter.”  Corroboration
was lacking given that the Crown had led no evidence of the respondent having appeared
to be intoxicated, or the like.
[6]
We allowed the Crown’s appeal.  We agreed with the advocate depute that the
procurator fiscal depute’s concession that there was no case to answer did not amount
to an unequivocal renunciation of the Crown’s right to prosecute the respondent.
Furthermore, that concession was not binding on the Crown and did not foreclose the
question of sufficiency (HMA v Paterson 2012 SCCR 621;  McLeod v Fraser 1986 SCCR 271).
The question of whether there was a sufficiency of evidence was a matter for the sheriff.  The
sheriff recognised this by carrying out her own assessment of sufficiency notwithstanding
the Crown’s concession.  For the respondent, Ms Culross did not seek to persuade us to any
contrary view.
[7]
Turning to the application of section 16 of the Act, whether the certificate was served
directly on the respondent or whether it was served indirectly by disclosure to his solicitors
was of no consequence, because the respondent’s solicitors challenged the certificate by
notice for the purposes of section 16(4) of the Act prior to the trial.  As a result of that
challenge, it was not open to the Crown to rely on section 16(1)(b) of the Act.  The certificate

4

could not therefore have been self-proving, in the absence of a witness to speak to its
contents.
[8]
However, the Crown called the toxicologist who had signed the certificate to speak
to its contents.  His evidence was given without objection and we are satisfied that, in
terms of section 16(5)(a) of the Act, his evidence was therefore sufficient evidence of the
facts stated in the certificate.  It was not necessary for the Crown to serve the certificate
on the respondent in terms of section 16(5)(b) of the Act in order to be able to rely on
section 16(5)(a).  Section 16(5)(a) and section 16(5)(b) of the Act deal with different situations:
subsection (5)(a) applies where the witness who signed the certificate gives evidence of the
contents of the certificate, whether or not the certificate has been served on the accused and,
if served, whether or not it is challenged in terms of subsection (4), whereas subsection (5)(b)
applies where a certificate is timeously served on the accused, is not challenged and is
therefore self-proving in terms of subsection (1)(b), even without a witness to speak to its
terms (Herron v Whitehill 1969 SLT 238;  MacNeill v Perrie 1981 SLT (Notes) 29;  McLeod v
Fraser).  In fairness to the sheriff, none of these authorities were cited to her by the Crown or
by the defence at the respondent’s trial.
[9]
The evidence of the toxicologist called by the Crown to speak to the terms of the
certificate at the respondent’s trial was, by virtue of section 16(5)(a) of the Act, sufficient
evidence of the facts stated in the certificate, namely the results of the analysis of the
respondent’s blood sample.  That evidence, along with the facts agreed by joint minute,
provided a sufficiency of evidence.  The procurator fiscal depute’s concession that there
was no case to answer was wrongly made and the submission of no case to answer should
have been repelled.

5

[10]
We therefore answered the single question posed in the stated case in the affirmative
and remitted the case to the sheriff to repel the submission of no case to answer and
thereafter to proceed as accords.
